title: PKU medical devices & hardware
source_note: Market/opportunity map of the hardware around PKU: the lab analyzers and dried-blood-spot systems that run newborn screening and monitoring, the mail-in DBS services patients use today, the point-of-care and at-home phe-testing efforts trying to close the biggest device gap in the disease, and the consumer scales repurposed for gram-level food weighing. Compiled July 2026 from manufacturer product pages (Revvity/PerkinElmer, Sciex, Baebies, Neoteryx, Etekcity/VeSync), the 2026 Nutrients review 'Point-of-Care Testing in PKU: A New ERA' (PMC12693881), the Egoo validation study (Orphanet JRD 2025 / NCT06940193), Aptatek/Lumos and Clemson/Circa press and ClinicalTrials.gov, and PKU-community monitoring guidance (PKU News, U-Washington, Alder Hey NHS). The through-line: there is still no cleared, commercially available home phe monitor in the US, the category-defining gap. Development stages are marked honestly; several highly visible efforts are research/clinical-stage, not products. Prices/turnaround are cited or marked estimate.

records.name: Home phenylalanine monitor
records.detail: There is no cleared, commercially available consumer device that lets a PKU patient measure blood phe at home the way a person with diabetes uses a glucometer or CGM. Monitoring still depends on dried-blood-spot cards mailed to a central lab, with results returning roughly 5-14 days later, so daily diet decisions are made blind.
records.market_signal: THE headline gap. PKU is the original newborn-screened disease yet has no home monitor 60+ years on; whoever ships a cleared, reimbursed at-home phe test owns a category with no incumbent and a built-in lifelong-adherence use case.

records.name: Egoo Phe System (P300 analyzer + Phe Test capsule + Collect board)
records.detail: CE-marked benchtop-to-home reader that runs an enzymatic, bioluminescent phe assay on ~40 uL of finger-prick blood; plasma is filtered on the Collect board and results appear in a Bluetooth smartphone app in ~29 minutes. Validation in PKU females showed strong agreement with dried blood spot (concordance ~0.91). Marketed as an adjunct to clinical monitoring, not a replacement.
records.market_signal: Closest thing to a real home phe test today, but CE-marked/EU only and not FDA-cleared for the US; a US regulatory + reimbursement path is the open lane. Currently in a US accuracy/usability trial (NCT06940193).

records.name: PheCheck (aptamer-based in-home phe monitor)
records.maker: Aptatek BioSciences (Columbia University spinout); development partner Lumos Diagnostics
records.detail: Handheld Bluetooth reader + single-use lateral-flow cartridge + phone app that uses DNA aptamers to quantify phe in ~5 uL of capillary blood, targeting a ~20-minute at-home result. Holds an FDA Breakthrough Device Designation. As of mid-2026 it is still in clinical development, not cleared: a PheCheck validation study (NCT07551921) was slated to start May 2026 with primary completion ~Dec 2026.
records.market_signal: The most advanced US-focused home-monitor bet, but repeatedly financed in bridge tranches and not yet cleared or launched. Execution/funding risk is the story; a successful 2026-2027 clearance would be the first true US home phe monitor.

records.name: At-home urine phe test (colorimetric dip disc + smartphone)
records.maker: Clemson University (LaTour lab); licensed to Circa Bioscience, LLC
records.detail: Low-cost urine test: a colorimetric disc is dipped in urine and photographed with a phone, reading the Fe3+/phenylpyruvic-acid color change (RGB) in about one minute to estimate blood phe. IRB clinical trial began 2019; reported to estimate blood phe within ~2.0 mg/dL at 90% confidence once individually correlated. Licensed to Circa Bioscience for commercialization; still pre-market.
records.market_signal: Cheapest, most patient-friendly form factor (urine, no lancet) and a plausible daily-use adherence tool, but it estimates rather than directly measures blood phe and needs per-patient calibration; commercialization has been slow.

records.name: PheCheck / ammonia-lyase self-monitoring method (PAL + portable ammonia detector)
records.maker: Academic (published method; uses a pre-existing portable ammonia detection system)
records.detail: Method that reacts phenylalanine ammonia-lyase (PAL) with a blood sample to release ammonia proportional to phe, then reads the ammonia on an existing portable detector. Distinct from the aptamer approach; demonstrates a repurposed-hardware route to home phe estimation.
records.market_signal: Illustrates that home phe sensing can piggyback on cheap, already-commercialized detector hardware rather than a bespoke reader; a low-capex path if accuracy holds.

sources.title: A method for phenylalanine self-monitoring using PAL and a portable ammonia detection system (PMC)

records.name: Aptamer-field-effect-transistor (Apta-FET) phe sensor
records.detail: Electronic biosensor that detects phe via an aptamer immobilized on a field-effect transistor, giving a direct electrical readout. Bench-stage proof of concept, not a packaged device.
records.market_signal: Represents the electrochemical/electronic-sensor lane (the CGM-style vision for phe). Years from product, but the closest conceptual analog to continuous glucose sensing.

sources.title: Phenylalanine Monitoring via Aptamer-Field-Effect-Transistor Sensors (ACS Sensors)

records.name: Whole-blood paper-based phe detection device
records.detail: Paper microfluidic device that performs enzymatic phe detection directly on whole blood for PKU therapy monitoring, aimed at a cheap disposable format. Laboratory proof of concept.
records.market_signal: Low-cost disposable chemistry is the commodity layer a home system needs; useful IP/partnering target rather than a standalone product.

sources.title: Development of a Whole Blood Paper-Based Device for Phenylalanine Detection (PMC)

records.name: Mitra VAMS (volumetric absorptive microsampling)
records.detail: Finger-prick collection device whose hydrophilic tip absorbs a precise 10-30 uL blood volume (tip self-indicates when full), improving on the variable-volume classic DBS card. Studied for PKU phe monitoring with strong concordance to plasma. Sample still ships to a lab for analysis.
records.market_signal: Upgrades the collection step but keeps the mail-to-lab loop; a bridge product, not a home reader. Signals demand for better-than-DBS sampling that a home device would ultimately displace.

sources.title: Point-of-Care Testing in PKU: A New ERA (Nutrients 2026) - VAMS/Mitra section

records.name: Dried blood spot (DBS) monitoring card + lancet kit
records.maker: Generic (Whatman/Ahlstrom 903 filter cards; supplied by clinics and screening labs)
records.detail: The standard at-home collection step: finger-prick, two hanging drops onto filter paper, air-dry, mail to a lab. Minimally invasive and cheap to produce, but the sample must travel and be assayed centrally, driving the multi-day results delay.
records.market_signal: The incumbent 'home' workflow is really a paper card plus the postal service. Its entire value proposition (cheap, mailable) is also its weakness (slow, no on-the-spot number) that a home reader attacks.

sources.title: Monitoring Blood Phenylalanine Levels at Home (Univ. of Washington)
Collection of blood spots for home monitoring of PKU (Alder Hey NHS)

records.name: Revvity PKU Monitoring (mail-in DBS service, test B0018)
records.detail: Central-lab service that measures phe (and typically tyrosine) on a mailed dried blood spot to track treatment and compliance in diagnosed PKU/hyperphenylalaninemia patients. Patient collects at home; lab runs and reports. Turnaround is a few lab days plus shipping, so real-world results land days after the stick.
records.market_signal: One of the dominant paid mail-in monitoring pipes. A large installed base of recurring, reimbursed testing is exactly the revenue an at-home device would try to convert or disintermediate.

sources.title: PKU Monitoring (Revvity test B0018)

records.name: Phenylalanine & Tyrosine, Self-Collect, Blood Spot (test PKUSC)
records.detail: Self-collected dried-blood-spot mail-in test for monitoring PKU therapy, measuring phe and tyrosine. Patient collects at home with the supplied kit and mails it in; reported turnaround on the order of ~3 lab days plus transit.
records.market_signal: Confirms mail-in phe monitoring is a routine catalog service across major reference labs, not a niche. The friction (kits, mailing, wait) is standardized and ripe to be collapsed by point-of-care.

sources.title: PKUSC - Phenylalanine and Tyrosine, Self-Collect, Blood Spot (Mayo Clinic Labs)

records.name: NHS home blood-spot PKU monitoring (clinic mail-in program)
records.maker: UK metabolic centres (e.g. Alder Hey Children's NHS Trust) via regional screening labs
records.detail: Publicly funded model where the clinic supplies blood-spot cards, the family collects on a set schedule at home, and cards are posted to the metabolic lab; results are phoned/messaged back and used to adjust diet. Same multi-day loop as the US commercial services but free at point of use.
records.market_signal: Shows the mail-in loop is the global default, funded either commercially (US) or by the state (UK/EU). A device play must fit both a fee-for-service and a single-payer reimbursement logic.

sources.title: Collection of blood spots for home monitoring of PKU (Alder Hey NHS)

records.name: NeoBase 2 Non-derivatized MSMS kit
records.detail: Tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS) reagent kit that quantifies phe and other amino acids/acylcarnitines from a single DBS punch, run on a triple-quadrupole instrument (e.g. Waters Xevo TQD). MS/MS is the most widely used first-tier method worldwide for phe determination in newborn screening.
records.market_signal: Core consumable of the centralized-lab status quo. High-throughput and accurate, but tethered to capital instruments and central labs, which is precisely why phe testing never left the building.

records.name: Neonatal Phenylalanine kit (fluorometric, NP-1000)
records.detail: Quantitative fluorometric microplate assay for phe in dried blood specimens, used as an aid in identifying PKU in newborns. The classic non-MS chemistry still run by many screening programs, especially outside high-resource MS/MS labs.
records.market_signal: The affordable lab workhorse for regions without mass spec. Its persistence shows how much of the world still runs plate-based lab chemistry, leaving point-of-care wide open globally.

sources.title: Neonatal Phenylalanine kit (960 tests, NP-1000) (Revvity)

records.name: GSP Instrument (Genetic Screening Processor)
records.detail: High-throughput automated batch analyzer for newborn screening on 96-well microplates from DBS, combining DELFIA immunoassay and enzymatic chemistries with automated plate handling. The dominant platform in medium-to-large public screening labs that a phe assay runs on.
records.market_signal: Capital-instrument backbone of centralized screening. Its dominance is the moat a home/point-of-care disruptor routes around rather than competes with head-on.

sources.title: GSP Instrument (IVD) (Revvity)

records.name: Sciex IVD-MS newborn screening solution (triple-quad MS/MS + amino-acid/acylcarnitine kit)
records.detail: Triple-quadrupole mass spectrometers plus a validated IVD reagent kit that quantify panels of amino acids (including phe) and acylcarnitines from a single DBS in one run, for clinical screening labs (CE-IVD in Europe).
records.market_signal: The other major MS/MS vendor in centralized screening. Confirms the lab-analyzer layer is a mature two-to-three-vendor oligopoly, with no consumer/home offering from any of them.

records.name: Quantase / Wallac phenylalanine enzymatic kit
records.maker: Bio-Rad (Quantase); Wallac (now Revvity) enzymatic phe kits
records.detail: Enzymatic/colorimetric phe assay (phenylalanine dehydrogenase, NAD+-linked) in microtitre-plate kit form for DBS, historically used to replace the Guthrie test for screening and monitoring. Still referenced in screening literature and comparisons.
records.market_signal: Legacy plate chemistry that unseated the Guthrie test decades ago; a reminder that phe testing has been re-platformed before, but always staying inside the lab.

records.name: Guthrie bacterial inhibition assay
records.maker: Originated by Robert Guthrie (1960s); historically kit-supplied by multiple vendors
records.detail: The original 1960s newborn-screening test: a DBS punch placed on agar seeded with Bacillus subtilis, where bacterial growth indicates elevated phe. Founded population newborn screening but is largely retired in favor of fluorometric and MS/MS methods.
records.market_signal: Historical anchor: it created the screened-newborn population that PKU care depends on, yet 60 years of lab innovation never produced a patient-held device. The unfinished job is home monitoring.

sources.title: Use of the Guthrie bacterial inhibition assay to monitor blood phe (ScienceDirect)

records.name: SEEKER (digital microfluidics newborn-screening platform)
records.detail: FDA-authorized digital-microfluidics platform that runs multiple enzyme assays from a single DBS punch; currently deployed for four lysosomal storage disorders in US newborn screening. Does not currently offer a phe/PKU assay, but its droplet-on-a-chip architecture is a candidate route to near-patient metabolic testing.
records.market_signal: Proof that miniaturized, chip-based DBS assays can win FDA clearance and enter screening labs. If pointed at phe, the platform (and its near-patient sibling below) is a credible disruption vector.

sources.title: Digital microfluidics comes of age (PubMed)

records.name: FINDER (near-patient testing device)
records.detail: Baebies' near-patient / point-of-care instrument built on the same digital-microfluidics core as SEEKER, positioned to bring DBS-style assays closer to the bedside/clinic. Not a PKU/phe product today.
records.market_signal: The most plausible corporate platform to add a point-of-care phe assay, since the microfluidics, DBS know-how, and regulatory experience already exist. A partnership/assay-add target worth watching.

records.name: Etekcity ESN00 Smart Nutrition Scale (Bluetooth food scale)
records.detail: Consumer Bluetooth kitchen scale (3 g-5000 g, 1 g increments, 4 sensors) that pairs to the VeSync app for macro/micronutrient lookups against a ~1M-food database. Repurposed by PKU families and the PKU Commons project (which integrates the ESN00 / FFF0-series scales) for gram-level protein/phe weighing, since the app's protein readout maps to phe budgeting.
records.market_signal: The de-facto PKU weighing device is a general-purpose consumer scale bent to the task via community tooling. No vendor markets to PKU, so the integration/data layer (not the hardware) is where value accrues.

sources.title: Etekcity ESN00 Smart Nutrition Scale (product page)
Etekcity ESN00 Smart Nutrition Scale review (Digital Trends)

records.name: PKU-purpose-built smart scale
records.detail: No scale is designed and sold for PKU. A purpose-built device would weigh in grams and surface phe (mg) per portion using a phe-aware food database and per-food phe factors, rather than the generic calorie/macro focus of consumer nutrition scales.
records.market_signal: A clean niche-hardware or software-plus-scale-bundle opportunity: PKU families already buy consumer scales and bolt on spreadsheets/apps; a phe-native scale or app-scale bundle would own the daily weighing ritual.

sources.title: Etekcity ESN00 (generic consumer scale used as the PKU stand-in)

records.name: Connected formula-preparation / dispenser hardware (e.g. Baby Brezza-class)
records.maker: Baby Brezza and other consumer infant-formula makers (no PKU-specific product)
records.detail: Automatic formula makers/dispensers mix powdered formula with heated water to a set consistency. General infant-formula devices exist and are patented, but none is built for metabolic (PKU) amino-acid formula, whose exact gram dosing and mixing needs differ. PKU caregivers still measure and mix by hand.
records.market_signal: Formula prep is a manual, precision-sensitive daily chore with no PKU-specific device. A metabolic-formula dispenser (accurate to the gram, dose-logged) is an untouched adjacent hardware gap.
